chapters.title: The Page That Hid
chapters.focus: irony and tone · idiom · implied meaning · sophisticated cohesion

pages.text: The Starlight Library had a reputation for swallowing visitors whole — not literally, the guidebooks hastened to add, but scholars who wandered in for an afternoon had been known to [[resurface|appear again after being gone a long time]] decades later, blinking and bearded. It was here, among a million muttering volumes, that the final page was said to lie.

q.q: What is the tone of the opening paragraph?
options: humorous exaggeration
genuine fear
dry scientific description
bitter criticism
q.explain: Scholars resurfacing “decades later, blinking and bearded” is comic exaggeration, and “not literally” winks at the reader.

pages.text: Its guardian, an ancient dragon called Vellum, was courteous to the point of [[absurdity|being silly or ridiculous]]. “By all means search,” he purred, “though I should warn you that the page has hidden itself. Pages do that, when they have been through a great deal. It will come out only for someone who has understood what the other five were trying to say.”

q.q: According to Vellum, what will make the page come out?
options: someone seeing what links the other pages
a careful search of every single shelf
the dragon's formal permission to take it
reading the five pages aloud in order
q.explain: “Only for someone who has understood what the other five were trying to say.”

pages.text: {hero} sat down and laid the five pages side by side. A sleepy meadow; a greedy little dragon forgiven; a riddle in a hollow tree; a serpent freed from somebody else's carelessness; a council talked round. It dawned on {hero} that not one page had been won by force. Each had been [[earned|got because you deserved it through your actions]] through kindness, patience or wit.

options: No page was won by force.
The pages follow a fixed order.
Each realm tried to keep its page.
Dragons appear in most chapters.
q.explain: “Not one page had been won by force. Each had been earned through kindness, patience or wit.”

pages.text: “Kindness, patience and wit,” {hero} said aloud. There was a rustle high above, and a page fluttered down like a falling leaf, settling in {hero}'s hands. Vellum inclined his great head. “Few manage it,” he said. “Most come looking for the page; you came looking for the point.” The Storybook closed with a contented sigh, whole at last — and {pet}, who had slept through the entire [[ordeal|a very difficult, unpleasant experience]], chose that moment to wake up.

q.q: What does Vellum mean by “you came looking for the point”?
options: {hero} sought the meaning, not the object.
{hero} wanted the sharpest page.
{hero} came to argue with him.
{hero} brought a map of the library.
q.explain: A play on words: others hunt the page itself; {hero} looked for its meaning (“the point”).

final.q: Why is {pet}'s waking up at the very end funny?
options: It sleeps through it all, then wakes when it's over.
It wakes just in time to find the page.
It finally frightens the dragon away.
It wakes up and reads the book aloud.
final.explain: Comic timing: {pet} misses the whole adventure and wakes the moment everything is solved.

chapters.title: The Book That Wouldn't End
chapters.focus: irony and understatement · idiom · implied meaning

pages.text: Vellum, it emerged, had a confession to make. Somewhere in the Starlight Library was a novel that refused to finish. Every time a reader reached its last page, a fresh chapter would [[sprout|appear and start growing suddenly]] from the spine, and the story would trundle on. “Delightful for the first three hundred years,” the dragon sighed, “somewhat less so since.”

q.q: What is Vellum's attitude to the endless book?
options: weary, expressed with dry humour
thrilled by its endless chapters
frightened of what it might do
indifferent, as if it hardly matters
q.explain: “Delightful for the first three hundred years… somewhat less so since” is understatement: he's tired of it, and says so wryly.

notes.thrilled by its endless chapters: “Somewhat less so since” tells us the delight wore off long ago.
notes.frightened of what it might do: He sighs; he isn't afraid. It's tiredness, not fear.
notes.indifferent, as if it hardly matters: He raised the problem himself, so it clearly matters to him.

pages.text: {hero} opened the book at random. It was, by any standard, a muddle: a princess who had been rescued eleven times, a villain who had retired, returned and retired again, and a talking teapot who appeared to have [[lost the thread|stopped following what was happening]] entirely. The characters seemed exhausted. One of them had written in the margin, in tiny letters: “Please let us stop.”

q.q: The note in the margin suggests that…
options: the characters themselves want the story to end
a previous reader scribbled a complaint
the teapot had written the whole book
the villain was hoping to come back for a third time
q.explain: It was written by “one of them”: the tired characters are asking for an ending.

notes.a previous reader scribbled a complaint: The text says “one of them”, meaning one of the exhausted characters.
notes.the teapot had written the whole book: The teapot had “lost the thread”. It isn't the author.
notes.the villain was hoping to come back for: The villain had already come back once. The note asks to stop, not to carry on.

pages.text: It struck {hero} that no one had ever asked the characters what ending they would like. Every reader had simply turned the page and hoped. So, with Vellum's [[blessing|permission and good wishes]], {hero} read the last page aloud and then asked, quite politely, what they wanted. The answer came at once, in a chorus of small voices: “A picnic. With everyone. And then nothing else at all.”

q.q: What did {hero} do that no reader had done before?
options: asked the characters how it should end
read the entire book cover to cover in one evening
wrote a brand-new final chapter
hid the book from the dragon
q.explain: “No one had ever asked the characters what ending they would like.”

notes.read the entire book cover to cover in o: {hero} only opened it “at random” and read the last page aloud.
notes.wrote a brand-new final chapter: {hero} didn't invent the ending. The characters chose it.
notes.hid the book from the dragon: {hero} acted “with Vellum's blessing”, not behind his back.

pages.text: {hero} wrote the picnic onto the last page in careful handwriting: the princess, the twice-retired villain and the teapot, sharing sandwiches on a hill. For a moment the book hesitated. Then it closed with a soft, [[contented|happy and satisfied]] thump, and no new chapter grew. “Three hundred years of plot,” Vellum murmured, “and all it wanted was lunch.” {pet}, curled on a cushion, slept through this chapter too.

q.q: Why is Vellum's final remark ironic?
options: A grand, endless story wanted something very ordinary.
Vellum had planned the picnic ending all along.
The characters were hungry because nobody had ever fed them.
The book had always been a cookbook in disguise.
q.explain: Three hundred years of plot, and the wish was just “lunch”: a huge story with a tiny, ordinary wish.

notes.Vellum had planned the picnic ending all: Vellum had no answer himself. It was {hero} who asked the characters.
notes.The characters were hungry because nobod: The joke isn't hunger. It's the gap between a huge story and a tiny wish.
notes.The book had always been a cookbook in d: It's a novel with a princess and a villain, not a cookbook.

final.q: If you have “lost the thread”, you have…
options: stopped following what is going on
dropped your sewing needle
run out of things to say
fallen out with a good friend
final.explain: Lost the thread = lost track of what is happening, like the muddled teapot.

notes.dropped your sewing needle: It's an idiom: there's no real thread or needle.
notes.run out of things to say: Close, but this idiom is about losing track of the story, not having nothing to say.
notes.fallen out with a good friend: That's a different idiom, about an argument.

pages.text: With the endless novel finally closed, the Starlight Library should, by any reasonable measure, have been peaceful. It was not. A narrow shelf near the back had begun to [[murmur|speak in a very soft voice]], just loudly enough to distract anyone trying to read nearby and just softly enough to deny doing so. “A minor inconvenience,” Vellum sighed, which, from a dragon who had endured three hundred years of plot, was saying rather a lot.

q.q: What is Vellum's attitude to the murmuring shelf?
options: dry understatement hiding irritation
delighted by a brand-new talking friend
terrified that the whole library will fall
completely uninterested in all the noise
q.explain: “A minor inconvenience,” after three hundred years of chaos, is understatement for real annoyance.

notes.delighted by a brand-new talking friend: He sighs; this is not delight.
notes.terrified that the whole library will fa: He calls it minor and sighs — tired irritation, not terror.
notes.completely uninterested in all the noise: He raised it himself, so it clearly bothers him.

pages.text: {hero} pressed an ear to the wood. The murmur resolved into hundreds of unfinished sentences, all talking over one another: characters from books that readers had abandoned halfway through a crisis. One knight kept asking where his horse had gone; a detective had [[lost the plot|stopped understanding the story — and, here, literally had no ending]] entirely. In the margin of a dusty atlas someone had scribbled, in a tiny hand: “We are still mid-chapter.”

q.q: The scribble “We are still mid-chapter” implies that…
options: the characters feel stuck mid-story
a careful librarian was taking notes for a catalogue
Vellum had written a long complaint about the noise
the atlas was made the loudest book on purpose
q.explain: The abandoned characters are speaking; “mid-chapter” means their stories were never finished.

notes.a careful librarian was taking notes for: The voices are the characters', not a librarian's catalogue notes.
notes.Vellum had written a long complaint abou: Vellum sighed about the noise; he didn't write in the atlas.
notes.the atlas was made the loudest book on p: The atlas holds the scribble; it isn't boasting about being loud.

pages.text: It occurred to {hero}, not for the first time in this library, that unfinished characters — like the endless novel's exhausted cast — might simply need to be asked. With Vellum's slightly [[wary|careful because you expect trouble]] blessing, {hero} tapped the shelf and enquired, quite politely, what would help. The answer arrived at once as a soft chorus: “A contents page. And permission to rest.”

q.q: What did {hero} do that changed the situation?
options: asked what the characters needed
rewrote every abandoned book in a single night
moved the noisy shelf out into the garden
told Vellum to burn all the noisy books
q.explain: As with the endless novel, asking was the step nobody had tried.

notes.rewrote every abandoned book in a single: {hero} asked; the characters named a contents page and rest — no full rewrite.
notes.moved the noisy shelf out into the garde: The shelf stayed in the library. The change was the question.
notes.told Vellum to burn all the noisy books: Nothing was burned. {hero} acted with Vellum's blessing to ask.

pages.text: {hero} wrote a single contents page listing every half-told tale under the heading “To Be Continued — Quietly”, slid it into the atlas, and closed the cover. For a moment the shelf hummed, as if checking the list twice. Then it fell silent, as contentedly as a cat in a sunbeam. “Three hundred years of noise,” Vellum murmured, “and all it wanted was a list.” {pet}, true to form, slept through the [[entire|whole, complete]] negotiation on a cushion labelled Returns.

q.q: Why is Vellum's final remark ironic?
options: A big mystery wanted only a simple list.
Vellum had prepared the contents page many weeks earlier.
The characters were noisy because they disliked all lists.
The atlas had always been a secret cookery book.
q.explain: A dramatic murmuring shelf, solved by a contents page: huge fuss, tiny ordinary wish.

notes.Vellum had prepared the contents page ma: Vellum had no answer ready; {hero} asked and wrote the page.
notes.The characters were noisy because they d: They asked for a contents page — they wanted the list.
notes.The atlas had always been a secret cooke: It's an atlas of unfinished tales, not a cookbook.

final.q: If someone has “lost the plot”, they have…
options: stopped understanding the story
dropped a detailed map behind a bookshelf
won a shiny prize for the very best story
finished every single chapter ahead of time
final.explain: Lost the plot = lost track of the story; here the detective also literally has no ending.

notes.dropped a detailed map behind a bookshel: It's an idiom about understanding, not a real map.
notes.won a shiny prize for the very best stor: The opposite of being confused or unfinished.
notes.finished every single chapter ahead of t: Lost the plot means confusion or no ending, not finishing early.

pages.text: With the murmuring shelf finally content, the Starlight Library should, by any reasonable measure, have erupted into celebration. It did not. Instead Vellum proposed — in the driest voice three centuries can manage — “a quiet reading hour,” as if silence itself were a daring new [[programme|a planned activity or event]]. “A modest idea,” he added, which, after the endless novel and the whispering shelf, was putting it mildly.

q.q: What is Vellum's tone about the quiet reading hour?
options: dry understatement after too much noise
wild excitement about a fireworks show
terror that the roof will collapse
boredom so deep he leaves the library
q.explain: Calling silence “a modest idea” after centuries of chaos is classic dry understatement.

notes.wild excitement about a fireworks show: He proposes quietly; this is not fireworks excitement.
notes.terror that the roof will collapse: He calls it modest — tired irony, not terror.
notes.boredom so deep he leaves the library: He stays to run the hour; he isn't walking out.

pages.text: {hero} chose a sunny window seat. Characters who had begged for a contents page now rested between covers, and the only sound was {pet} turning a page with surprising care. In the margin of a poetry chapbook someone had written, in the same tiny hand: “We are [[between chapters|in a peaceful pause before the next part]].” It was hard not to smile.

q.q: The scribble “We are between chapters” implies that…
options: the characters feel peacefully paused
a librarian was counting every chair for stock
Vellum had banned all reading forever
the poetry book wanted to start a loud parade
q.explain: After “mid-chapter” panic, “between chapters” suggests a calm pause the characters accept.

notes.a librarian was counting every chair for: The voices asked for rest; this is their peaceful note, not stock-taking.
notes.Vellum had banned all reading forever: Vellum invited a reading hour; he didn't ban reading.
notes.the poetry book wanted to start a loud p: A quiet hour is the opposite of a loud parade.

pages.text: It occurred to {hero} that the library's greatest dramas had ended the same way: not with a flourish, but with someone finally asking what was needed. Vellum, slightly less [[wary|careful because you expect trouble]] than before, even read aloud a short poem about rain on quiet roofs. Nobody interrupted. The shelf did not murmur. The atlas stayed shut.

q.q: What pattern does {hero} notice about the library's dramas?
options: they ended when someone asked what was needed
they ended only when every book was burned
they ended when the fog bell rang across a lake
they ended when kites tangled over a picnic
q.explain: Asking helped the endless novel and the shelf; {hero} notices that pattern.

notes.they ended only when every book was burn: Nothing was burned. Asking was the turning point.
notes.they ended when the fog bell rang across: The fog bell is another realm's story.
notes.they ended when kites tangled over a pic: Kite tangles were at Cloud Castle, not this pattern.

pages.text: When the hour closed, Vellum stamped a small card for {hero}: Guest of the Quiet Hour. “Three hundred years of plot,” he murmured, “and the twist was simply… rest.” {pet}, having slept through half the poems on the Returns cushion, woke only for the stamp's soft thud — timing that was, Vellum noted dryly, [[impeccable|perfectly well timed]].

q.q: Why is Vellum's remark about “the twist was simply rest” ironic?
options: A huge saga wanted only ordinary quiet.
He had planned a fireworks finale all along.
The characters demanded louder plots forever.
The stamp card was secretly a cookery recipe.
q.explain: Centuries of dramatic noise, solved by rest: enormous fuss, tiny ordinary wish — again.

notes.The characters demanded louder plots for: They asked for rest and a contents page, not louder plots.
notes.The stamp card was secretly a cookery re: It's a guest card, not a recipe.

options: perfectly well timed
hopelessly late and messy
written in a secret code
loud enough to wake the whole shelf
final.explain: Impeccable = perfectly well timed — like {pet} waking exactly for the stamp.

notes.hopelessly late and messy: The opposite of late and messy.
notes.written in a secret code: Impeccable is about quality of timing, not a code.
notes.loud enough to wake the whole shelf: The stamp was soft; impeccable isn't about volume.
